paragraphs: The heir to Lambton, the fine estate and hall beside the swift-flowing Wear, was a wild young man. He would never attend Mass at Brugeford Chapel on a Sunday. Instead, he went fishing. And if he caught nothing, people passing on their way to Brugeford could hear him cursing.

Well, one Sunday morning he was fishing as usual, but not a single salmon had risen to his bait, and his basket held neither roach nor dace. The worse his luck grew, the worse his language became, until the people passing on their way to hear the priest say Mass were horrified by his words.

At last young Lambton felt a mighty tug on his line. “At last,” he said, “a bite worth having!” He pulled and pulled, until a head like an elf’s appeared above the water, with nine holes on each side of its mouth. Still he pulled, until he dragged the thing ashore. It proved to be a hideously shaped Worm. If he had cursed before, his curses now were enough to make your hair stand on end.
“What is troubling you, my son?” said a voice beside him. “And what have you caught that makes you stain the Lord’s Day with such foul language?”
Young Lambton looked around and saw a strange old man standing beside him.
“Why, honestly,” he said, “I think I have caught the devil himself. Look and see whether you recognise him.”

But the stranger shook his head. “It means no good for you or your family to bring such a monster ashore,” he said. “Yet do not throw him back into the Wear. You have caught him, and you must keep him.” With that, he turned away and was never seen again.
The young heir of Lambton picked up the gruesome thing, took it off his hook, and threw it into a nearby well. Ever since that day, the well has been called the Worm Well.

For some time, nothing more was seen or heard of the Worm. Then one day it had grown too large for the well and emerged, fully grown. It left the well and made its way to the Wear. All day it lay coiled around a rock in the middle of the river. At night it came out of the water and ravaged the countryside. It sucked the cows’ milk, devoured the lambs, attacked the cattle, and frightened all the women and girls in the district. Then it withdrew for the rest of the night to the hill still called the Worm Hill, on the north side of the Wear, about a mile and a half from Lambton Hall.

This terrible affliction brought young Lambton of Lambton Hall to his senses. He took the vows of a crusader and left for the Holy Land, hoping that the scourge he had brought upon his district would disappear. But the grisly Worm paid no attention. Instead, it crossed the river and came right up to Lambton Hall itself. The old lord lived there all alone, his only son having gone to the Holy Land. What could they do? The Worm came closer and closer to the Hall. Women shrieked, men gathered weapons, dogs barked, and horses neighed in terror. At last the steward called to the dairymaids, “Bring all your milk here!” They brought all the milk the nine cows in the cowshed had given, and he poured it into the long stone trough in front of the Hall.

The Worm came nearer and nearer until it reached the trough. When it smelled the milk, it turned aside to the trough and swallowed every drop. Then it slowly turned around, crossed the River Wear, and coiled its great body three times around the Worm Hill for the night.

After that, the Worm crossed the river every day, and woe to the Hall if the trough held the milk of fewer than nine cows. The Worm would hiss and rage and lash its tail around the trees in the park. In its fury it uprooted the stoutest oaks and the tallest firs. This went on for seven years. Many people tried to destroy the Worm, but all failed. Many a knight lost his life fighting the monster, which slowly crushed the life out of everyone who came near it.

At last the young heir of Lambton returned to his father’s Hall after seven long years of meditation and repentance on holy soil. He found his people sad and desolate. The fields lay unploughed, the farms were deserted, and half the trees in the park had been uprooted, because no one would stay to tend the nine cows whose milk the monster needed every day.
The young heir went to his father and begged forgiveness for the curse he had brought upon the Hall.
“Your sin is forgiven,” his father said. “But go to the Wise Woman of Brugeford and find out whether anything can free us from this monster.”
The young heir went to the Wise Woman and asked her advice.
“It is your fault that we suffer, young man,” she said. “Let it be you who frees us.”
“I would give my life,” he said.

“Perhaps you will,” she said. “But listen to me, and listen carefully. You, and you alone, can kill the Worm. To do so, go to the blacksmith and have your armour studded with spearheads. Then go to the Worm’s Rock in the Wear and take your place there. When the Worm comes to the rock at dawn, try your strength against him, and may God bring you safely through.”
“I will do this,” young Lambton said.

“But one thing more,” the Wise Woman said as she returned to her little dwelling. “If you kill the Worm, swear that you will put to death the first thing that meets you as you cross the threshold of Lambton Hall again. Do this, and all will be well with you and your family. Fail to keep your vow, and for three times three generations, none of the Lambtons will die in his bed. Swear it, and do not fail.”

The young heir swore as the Wise Woman told him and went to the blacksmith. There he had his armour studded all over with spearheads. Then he kept his prayer vigil in Brugeford Chapel, and at daybreak took his place on the Worm’s Rock in the River Wear.

As dawn broke, the Worm unwound its snakelike coils from the hill and came to its rock in the river. When it saw the young heir waiting, it lashed the water in fury, wrapped its coils around him, and tried to crush him to death. But the harder it squeezed, the deeper the spearheads dug into its sides. Still it squeezed and squeezed, until all the water around it was red with blood. Then the Worm unwound itself, leaving the young heir free to use his sword. He raised it, brought it down, and cut the Worm in two. One half fell into the river and was swiftly carried away. Once more, the head and the rest of the body coiled around him, but with less strength, and the spearheads did their work. At last the Worm unwound, snorted out its last foam of blood and fire, and rolled dying into the river. It was never seen again.

The young heir of Lambton swam ashore, lifted his bugle to his lips, and sounded it three times. This was the signal to the Hall, where the servants and the old lord had shut themselves in to pray for his success. At the third note, they were to release Boris, his favourite hound. But they were so delighted to hear that the young heir was safe and the Worm defeated that they forgot their orders. When he reached the threshold of the Hall, his old father rushed out to meet him and was about to clasp him to his breast.

“The vow! The vow!” cried the young heir of Lambton, and blew another blast on his horn. This time the servants remembered and released Boris, who came bounding towards his young master. The young heir raised his shining sword and cut off his faithful hound’s head.

But the vow had been broken, and for nine generations no man of the Lambton family died in his bed. The last of the Lambtons died in his carriage while crossing Brugeford Bridge, one hundred and thirty years ago.
